Claim: The bone is a baboon fibula.
Source URL/archive: MAA Convergence (secondary, 'probably a fibula of a baboon, large cat, or other large mammal'); https://www.bibnum.education.fr/sites/default/files/ishango-analysis_v2.pdf (saved sources/keller_ishango_analysis_v2.pdf)
Page/passage: Keller p.12 (the baboon fibula he mentions is the Lebombo bone, Bogoshi, Naidoo & Webb 1987, not Ishango)
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): Brochure p.18: "The bone handle has been narrowed, scraped, polished and engraved, so we can no longer tell what kind of bone it is, although we do know it belonged to a mammal." Smithsonian: "This fossil mammal bone".
Disagreement/limits: The holding institution says the species cannot be identified. 'Baboon fibula' seems to come from confusion with the Lebombo bone (South Africa) or loose popular retelling.
Permitted narration: Say 'a mammal bone' only. Do not name a species.

Claim: It carries 168 notches in three columns on three sides of the handle.
Source URL/archive: RBINS/ADIA brochure 'Have you heard of Ishango?' (2024) https://www.naturalsciences.be/file/cc73d96153bbd5448a56f19d925d05b1379c7f21/369895724a871d793f603e27d8e31fae74fdbf13/inst-202403-brochure-ishango-en-fv.pdf (saved sources/inst_brochure_ishango_en.pdf)
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): "The handle is carved with 168 parallel marks... on three sides of the handle."
Disagreement/limits: Count depends on how worn or ambiguous marks are read (see C09, D06). 168 = 60 + 48 + 60 (arithmetic checked).
Permitted narration: The museum counts 168 marks, cut in three columns along the handle.

Source URL/archive: RBINS/ADIA brochure 'Have you heard of Ishango?' (2024) https://www.naturalsciences.be/file/cc73d96153bbd5448a56f19d925d05b1379c7f21/369895724a871d793f603e27d8e31fae74fdbf13/inst-202403-brochure-ishango-en-fv.pdf (saved sources/inst_brochure_ishango_en.pdf) ; https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00860v2 (saved sources/pletser_huylebrouck_2016_v2.pdf) ; https://www.bibnum.education.fr/sites/default/files/ishango-analysis_v2.pdf (saved sources/keller_ishango_analysis_v2.pdf)
Author/date: RBINS/ADIA 2024; Pletser & Huylebrouck 2016; de Heinzelin 1962 quoted by Keller
Page/passage: Brochure p.19 diagram; P&H p.17 schematic; Keller pp.4-5
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): Brochure p.19 diagram gives the groups and "The total number of lines in each column is a multiple of twelve." P&H p.17: "sums... are 60, 48 and 60", annotating middle groups as "10 (9+1 ?)" and "5 (1+4 ?)".
Disagreement/limits: Keller p.5: "one of the sets of 5 is genuinely illegible, and in reality the 10 could be a 9". Rosenberg (Cabinet) transcribes the middle as 3, 5, 4, 8... (likely a transcription error). Order and column labels vary between sources.
Permitted narration: As the museum reads them, the columns hold groups of 11, 13, 17 and 19; 3, 6, 4, 8, 10, 5, 5 and 7; and 11, 21, 19 and 9 notches. Some marks are worn, so a few counts are uncertain.

Claim: The museum's own description of the groupings (doubling pattern).
Source URL/archive: https://www.naturalsciences.be/en/museum/exhibitions-activities/exhibitions/250-years-of-natural-sciences/the-ishango-bone (Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels; saved sources/museum.html)
Author/date: Institute of Natural Sciences web page
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): "What makes it unique are the notches that appear to be grouped together. On one side, for example, there are groups of three and six (2 x 3), four and eight (2 x 4), and five and ten (2 x 5) notches."
Disagreement/limits: Note the hedge 'appear to be'. The pairs are an observation; what they mean is debated (D01-D06).
Permitted narration: In the museum's words, the notches 'appear to be grouped', with pairs such as three and six, four and eight, five and ten.

Claim: De Heinzelin's reading: an 'arithmetical game' showing duplication, numbers based on 10, and possibly primes.
Source URL/archive: https://www.bibnum.education.fr/sites/default/files/ishango-analysis_v2.pdf (saved sources/keller_ishango_analysis_v2.pdf) ; https://www.cabinetmagazine.org/issues/28/rosenberg.php
Author/date: J. de Heinzelin, Scientific American 206(6), June 1962, p.105ff (doi 10.1038/scientificamerican0662-105), quoted by Keller pp.4-5 and Rosenberg
Page/passage: Keller pp.4-5; Cabinet citing SciAm pp.109-110
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): "This arrangement strongly suggests appreciation of the concept of duplication... It is of course possible that all the patterns are fortuitous. But it seems probable that they were deliberately planned. If so, they may represent an arithmetical game of some sort, devised by a people who had a number system based on 10 as well as a knowledge of duplication and of prime numbers."
Disagreement/limits: Criticised by Keller (pp.4-5, 13, 16) and rejected on primes by Pletser & Huylebrouck. De Heinzelin himself hedged ('possible that all the patterns are fortuitous'; 1957: no logical way to prove it isn't chance, quoted P&H p.19).
Permitted narration: Its finder suggested the marks might be an arithmetic game, though he admitted they might be chance.

Claim: The left column (11, 13, 17, 19) shows knowledge of prime numbers.
Source URL/archive: https://www.bibnum.education.fr/sites/default/files/ishango-analysis_v2.pdf (saved sources/keller_ishango_analysis_v2.pdf) ; https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00860v2 (saved sources/pletser_huylebrouck_2016_v2.pdf) ; RBINS/ADIA brochure 'Have you heard of Ishango?' (2024) https://www.naturalsciences.be/file/cc73d96153bbd5448a56f19d925d05b1379c7f21/369895724a871d793f603e27d8e31fae74fdbf13/inst-202403-brochure-ishango-en-fv.pdf (saved sources/inst_brochure_ishango_en.pdf)
Page/passage: Keller p.4; P&H p.17, pp.19-20; brochure p.20
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): P&H p.17: "rejected others (such as the one of prime numbers)". Brochure p.20: not enough proof to confirm an understanding of prime numbers.
Disagreement/limits: Even proponents of a numerical reading reject this. P&H read 11,13,17,19 as 12-1,12+1,18-1,18+1.
Permitted narration: The numbers 11, 13, 17 and 19 happen to be primes. Most researchers doubt the carvers meant that.

Claim: It is a counting tool mixing bases 10 and 12 -- 'the oldest mathematical tool of humankind'.
Source URL/archive: https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00860v2 (saved sources/pletser_huylebrouck_2016_v2.pdf)
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): "...yielding an unspectacular conclusion: it is probably a tool that counts events or things, noted by someone who mixed bases 10 and 12." Abstract: "the oldest mathematical tool of humankind. Our hypothesis, that is widely accepted..."
Disagreement/limits: 'Widely accepted' is the authors' own claim. Keller rejects the premise that the notches are numbers at all.
Permitted narration: Some mathematicians argue it was a counting tool, perhaps mixing tens and twelves.

Claim: Marshack's reading: a lunar calendar/notation.
Source URL/archive: https://www.cabinetmagazine.org/issues/28/rosenberg.php ; RBINS/ADIA brochure 'Have you heard of Ishango?' (2024) https://www.naturalsciences.be/file/cc73d96153bbd5448a56f19d925d05b1379c7f21/369895724a871d793f603e27d8e31fae74fdbf13/inst-202403-brochure-ishango-en-fv.pdf (saved sources/inst_brochure_ishango_en.pdf)
Author/date: A. Marshack, Science 146 (1964) 743-745; The Roots of Civilization (1972) -- not read first-hand
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): Brochure p.20: Marshack "also believes it is a system of number notation, but one which is related to the lunar calendar."
Disagreement/limits: Keller p.4 fn4: "Marshack's interpretation of the bone as a lunar calendar, which is now largely discredited." d'Errico 1989 'Palaeolithic Lunar Calendars: A Case of Wishful Thinking?' Current Anthropology 30(1) (title only read). Rosenberg: Marshack's figures 'hardly less numerological'.
Permitted narration: One researcher argued it tracked the phases of the moon; most specialists don't accept that.

Claim: The marks are tallies (one mark per thing counted).
Source URL/archive: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/behavior/recording-information/ishango-bone ; RBINS/ADIA brochure 'Have you heard of Ishango?' (2024) https://www.naturalsciences.be/file/cc73d96153bbd5448a56f19d925d05b1379c7f21/369895724a871d793f603e27d8e31fae74fdbf13/inst-202403-brochure-ishango-en-fv.pdf (saved sources/inst_brochure_ishango_en.pdf)
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): Smithsonian: "three rows of tally marks... They may have been used to add or multiply."
Disagreement/limits: Smithsonian hedges ('may'); Keller warns a tally/bijection 'is not a number' (p.16).
Permitted narration: Many think the marks record a count of something; nobody knows what.

Claim: Sceptical reading: the marks may not be numbers at all; modern readers project maths onto them.
Source URL/archive: https://www.bibnum.education.fr/sites/default/files/ishango-analysis_v2.pdf (saved sources/keller_ishango_analysis_v2.pdf)
Author/date: Olivier Keller, 'The fables of Ishango, or the irresistible temptation of mathematical fiction', BibNum (English PDF 2015)
Evidence type: Critical essay (not peer-reviewed; P&H criticise it as such)
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): p.4: "Several of the notches are worn way or barely visible, which immediately makes any numeric interpretation suspect." p.5: "Once it has been decided that the sets of notches are numbers, it's easy... to load the bone with meaning". p.13: "A notch may be nothing more than a mark".
Disagreement/limits: P&H 2016 dispute Keller strongly. Brochure p.20 summarises his caution fairly.
Permitted narration: Sceptics warn we may be reading our own maths into the marks.
Status (SOURCED / CONTESTED / UNVERIFIED: SOURCED (Keller text read; reading itself CONTESTED)

(2024) https://www.naturalsciences.be/file/cc73d96153bbd5448a56f19d925d05b1379c7f21/369895724a871d793f603e27d8e31fae74fdbf13/inst-202403-brochure-ishango-en-fv.pdf (saved sources/inst_brochure_ishango_en.pdf) ; https://www.cabinetmagazine.org/issues/28/rosenberg.php

Claim: The notches are just grip or decoration.
Source URL/archive: (none found)
Supporting evidence (verbatim quote): De Heinzelin 1962 (via Cabinet, p.110): "The pattern of these notches leads me to suspect that they represent more than pure decoration."
Disagreement/limits: No source read that argues grip; decoration is only mentioned as the alternative de Heinzelin rejected.

Claim: The Ishango bone proves Africans invented mathematics / is 'the oldest mathematical object'.
Source URL/archive: https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00860v2 (saved sources/pletser_huylebrouck_2016_v2.pdf) ; https://www.bibnum.education.fr/sites/default/files/ishango-analysis_v2.pdf (saved sources/keller_ishango_analysis_v2.pdf)
Page/passage: P&H abstract ('oldest mathematical tool' as hypothesis); Keller p.2 (museum once billed it 'humanity's oldest calculator')
Disagreement/limits: Hypothesis, not proof. The Lebombo bone and other notched objects are older. Present museum page doesn't use 'oldest calculator'.
Permitted narration: It is among the oldest objects that some researchers read as mathematical.

Claim: Its meaning was hidden or suppressed.
Source URL/archive: (none found)
Disagreement/limits: No evidence in any source read; the bone has been on public display and widely published since 1957-62.
